blocks.text: Have you ever wondered why some variables seem to disappear while others persist throughout your code? Understanding scope and lifetime is crucial to managing your program's variables effectively.

blocks.markdown: In programming, understanding where a variable is accessible and how long it exists are fundamental concepts. These are known as **scope** and **lifetime**, respectively. This lesson will explore these concepts, highlighting their importance and potential pitfalls, especially when dealing with global variables.

blocks.title: Scope
blocks.text: Scope refers to the region of the program where a variable is accessible. It determines which parts of your code can 'see' or use a variable.

blocks.title: Lifetime
blocks.text: Lifetime refers to the duration for which a variable exists in memory during the execution of a program.

blocks.markdown: The scope of a variable is defined by where it is declared. In most programming languages, there are two main types of scope: **local** and **global**.

items: Local Scope: Variables declared within a function have local scope. They are only accessible within that function.
Global Scope: Variables declared outside any function have global scope. They are accessible throughout the program.

blocks.title: Example of Local Scope
blocks.prompt: Consider the following code snippet. Determine the scope of the variable `x`.

steps.text:
```python
 def my_function():
     x = 10
     print(x)
 my_function()
 print(x)  # What will this print?
 ```
The variable `x` is declared inside `my_function`. Therefore, it has local scope.
When `my_function()` is called, it prints the value of `x`, which is `10`.
The line `print(x)` outside the function will cause an error because `x` is not defined in the global scope.

blocks.answer: The variable `x` is only accessible within `my_function`. Attempting to print `x` outside the function results in an error.

blocks.title: Example of Global Scope
blocks.prompt: Consider this code snippet. Determine the scope of the variable `y`.

steps.text:
```python
 y = 5
 def another_function():
     print(y)
 another_function()
 print(y)
 ```
The variable `y` is declared outside any function, giving it global scope.
Both `another_function()` and the line `print(y)` outside the function can access `y`.

blocks.answer: The variable `y` is accessible both inside `another_function()` and outside it, as it has global scope.

blocks.title: Warning About Global Variables
blocks.text: Using global variables can make programs difficult to understand and debug because any part of the code can change their value.

blocks.markdown: Now, let's explore the concept of lifetime. A variable's lifetime is often tied to its scope, but they are not the same. A variable with local scope typically has a lifetime that ends when the function returns, while a global variable's lifetime lasts for the duration of the program.

blocks.title: Local Variable Lifetime
blocks.text: A local variable is created when the function is called and destroyed when the function exits.

blocks.title: Global Variable Lifetime
blocks.text: A global variable is created when the program starts and destroyed when the program ends.

points: Scope determines where a variable is accessible in the code.
Lifetime determines how long a variable exists in memory.
Global variables can lead to complex dependencies and bugs.
